marketdesk-1x8fde7d63g-040a6f: The AI build-out is changing the rules
Hyperscalers can still fund massive AI investment, but markets are becoming far less willing to ignore the cost.

While hyperscalers have strong balance sheets and ample financial flexibility, the market is becoming less forgiving of ever-rising AI spending. The pressure is already visible in credit markets. Meta's $27.3 billion Hyperion financing was issued at par, traded above 109, and has since fallen to around 97. The broader concern is deteriorating free cash flow conversion as capex accelerates. Increasingly, investing in hyperscalers is a bet that AI revenues ramp before spending peaks. If not, today's capacity build could become tomorrow's compute oversupply, just as much larger depreciation charges begin flowing through income statements writes Privorotsky.

Google encapsulated the market's growing concern around AI spending. Despite reporting excellent operating results, including 82% Cloud growth, Alphabet fell 6.9% after raising 2026 capex guidance to $195–205 billion and posting negative quarterly free cash flow of $5.9 billion. Investors are becoming less willing to treat AI spending as costless, particularly as questions around long-term returns remain unanswered. More importantly, higher spending by Google raises the bar for the rest of the hyperscalers, increasing pressure across the sector, writes Privorotsky. Note GOOG closed below the 200 day MA for the first time since last June.

The Magnificent Seven remain cash-flow machines, but their massive AI build-out is making them increasingly sensitive to rates, all else equal. The first chart compares MAGS, not a perfect proxy for the hyperscalers, but a reasonable one, to the inverse of the US 10-year yield. The second compares MAGS with bond volatility, which has moved almost perfectly inversely with the basket. As AI capex accelerates, the market is increasingly treating hyperscalers less like traditional cash-generative tech and more like long-duration assets.

AI is no longer just driving equity markets, it's reshaping credit. Goldman Sachs notes that investment- grade issuance is increasingly outpacing US Treasury supply, fueled by record debt issuance from AI hyperscalers. The question is no longer whether they can borrow, but whether this torrent of new bonds starts crowding out the rest of the market.

Credit spreads suggest investors are becoming more cautious about the economics of AI spending, yet equity valuations remain far more forgiving. Should stocks begin converging with credit, there may still be meaningful downside for hyperscaler equities.

announcement, Iyogin HD plans to conclude a share exchange agreement with Ehime Bank in December, followed by an extraordinary general meeting of Ehime Bank shareholders in February 2027, with the share exchange scheduled to take effect on April 1, 2027. According to the disclosure materials (Japanese only), the two entities’ combined lending share in Ehime Prefecture is 51.0% and their deposit share is 52.6% (as of the end of March 2025), and both banks possess strengths in ship finance (as of December 2025, Iyo Bank ranks 3rd domestically and 10th globally in ship finance balance, while Ehime Bank ranks 12th domestically and 37th globally). Furthermore, according to various media reports, their combined share of main bank corporate clients would reach 76% (based on 2025 data).

As for synergy effects expected from the integration, the disclosure materials cite regional contributions, as well as the integration of administrative operations and systems, unification of products and services, and the centralization and streamlining of branch and headquarter operations.

Our view: Regional bank integration and mergers are currently accelerating in Japan, backed by policy support such as a special law exempting regional bank integrations and mergers from the Antimonopoly Act, as well as support grants for regional bank realignment (up to ¥5 bn). Costs related to system renewals and regional bank realignment in neighboring areas could also serve as tailwinds pushing regional banks to consider realignment. We include a regional bank map below. Cases of realignment among independent banks or re-realignment of already integrated entities are also beginning to emerge as consolidation progresses, and we continue to keep a close watch on this as an investment theme in the banking sector.

Trading times Blog Paul Donovan, Chief Economist, UBS GWM, UBS AG London Branch

The volume of global trade as a share of the world economy has risen for ten consecutive quarters, and is now the highest proportion of world economy activity in modern times. How is this possible in an era of tariffs and trade wars? Three reasons stand out.
Generally, trade wars are a US affair. Most of the rest of the world has continued to trade nicely with one another. The US is an important consumer market, but is not everything.

The US consumer has shown considerable reluctance to cut imports. The act of threatening tariffs before they take effect creates a lot of noise in data, but broadly, the US is importing about as much today as it did in 2024. The seemingly insatiable demand for artificial intelligence is part of that resilience.

There is evidence that tariffs are being avoided. Comparing China’s export data and US import data shows that China claims to be exporting 30% more value to the US than the US claims to be importing from China. This is not because 30% of ships are sinking mid-Pacific. This level of distortion is unique to Sino-US trade. If imports from China are not identified as coming from China, the importer may pay a lower (or no) tax.

marketdesk-9ih2z5xd9ca-f48984: The Most Fundamental Macro Risk Is Back

BY TYLER DURDEN THURSDAY, JUL 23, 2026 - 03:10 PM Authored by Simon White, Bloomberg macro strategist, Rising inflation volatility is set to trigger earnings disappointments, wider credit spreads and more variability in stock and bond prices. Inflation is on the cusp of reigniting, as the incessant conflict in the Middle East takes oil prices back towards $100. That’s not good news, but more troubling for markets is that the volatility of inflation is also sharply rising again. It is the ultimate macro risk, as everything – goods prices, borrowing rates, Federal Reserve policy and cash flows – becomes more uncertain when the purchasing power of money itself becomes unstable. Higher inflation alone is pernicious for the performance of risk assets. But the increase in the variability of CPI prints, which last month’s lower-than-expected outturn exemplifies, allows counter-narratives to persist that the inflation regime is ending. That adds to market volatility and drives up risk premia. The pick-up in inflation vol is becoming increasingly apparent at the top level, but it is unmistakable under the surface. The average volatility across US CPI components is close to revisiting the highs of the pandemic price surge.

The impact of inflation volatility on consumption is well documented. The Katona effect, named after the behavioural economist George Katona, describes how consumers postpone expenditures when inflation and its volatility rise. But there is no similar well-defined neologism for inflation volatility’s effect on markets. There should be though, as it is every bit as important. The combination of growing price pressures – with their leeching effect on market-supporting liquidity – and the increased uncertainty of higher inflation vol are toxic for risk premia. The two often go together: inflation exhibits heteroskedasticity, ie its variance rises as it increases. That’s clear as day if we split US CPI into deciles, with the highest decile having by far the largest inflation volatility on average.

its two-month correlation with the Nasdaq 100 has fallen to its lowest level in more than 15 years, reinforcing its role as the market's preferred defensive mega-cap.
Meta continues to trade within the same broad range that has contained price action since September 2024. Until that range breaks, the technical picture remains neutral.

HPCL’s 1Q Goldman Sachs (Singapore) Pte loss represented ~20% of FY26 book value. We believe upside risks to oil prices (escalating geopolitical tensions) and further downside risks to marketing margins in coming quarters are again top of mind for investors. Our Commodities team sees two-sided oil price risks but skewed to the upside on net, especially in the near term where Brent could exceed US$120/bbl in Dec’26 quarter and average US$100/bbl in CY27 if Hormuz remains disrupted through CY27, with further upside if the Bab-al-Mandab Strait and Suez are also permanently disrupted. On the other hand, Brent might decline to the low US$60s by end-CY27 if supply exceeds our expectations and demand losses prove more persistent.

We estimate HPCL and BPCL shares are already pricing in a normalization of integrated margins assuming mid-cycle multiples. We do not see a compelling risk reward with 44%/46% up/downside in our bull / bear case scenarios on average for HPCL/BPCL. We cut estimates further in the near term, remain below Bloomberg consensus for FY27E EBITDA and broadly maintain our medium-term assumptions for both marketing margins (assumes normal margins by FY29E) and refining margins (above mid-cycle margins through FY29E). Thought of the day US Treasury yields are approaching their recent highs in May as escalating hostilities in the Middle East and rising energy prices have rekindled inflation fears and concerns that the Federal Reserve may need to raise policy rates in the near term. The 10-year Treasury yield stood at 4.7% at the time of writing, surpassing its May peak of 4.68%.

Media reports said that the Iran-aligned Houthis attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea as part of a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, disrupting another vital waterway for global energy supplies. The US has continued its strikes to “further degrade” Iran’s ability to threaten ship traffic, while Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warned that no tanker would be allowed to enter or leave the Strait of Hormuz without coordination with the Islamic Republic. Brent crude oil was trading above USD 100/bbl at the time of writing, having risen by over 37% since the start of this month.

But we continue to see scope for yields to drift lower over the coming quarters, and believe quality fixed income offers an attractive combination of income, diversification, and medium-term return potential.

Energy disruptions from the Middle East should ease over time. Investors should be prepared for further hostilities, with regional mediators’ ongoing attempts to bring the US and Iran back to the negotiating table so far proving unsuccessful. But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the US remains open to a diplomatic solution, and US President Trump this week claimed that oil prices will go down, saying “just give me a little time.” Our view remains that the US and Iran will eventually seek a path toward a diplomatic framework as economic pressures mount, and that oil prices could return to levels that would keep inflation under control.

Thought of the day The European Central Bank left the deposit rate unchanged at 2.25% at its July meeting, a widely anticipated decision after June’s 25-basis-point increase. The overall message from both the statement and press conference was that of a hawkish hold, with policymakers expressing concern about the inflationary consequences of higher energy prices. The re-escalation in the US-Iran conflict has pushed European natural gas futures to a four-month high, while Brent crude oil prices hit USD 100/bbl for the first time in two months.

With energy prices rising again, ECB policymakers appear to have moved away from the more balanced risk assessment discussed at the Sintra forum and back toward a framework of upside risks to inflation and downside risks to economic growth.
We continue to expect the ECB to raise policy rates by 25bps in September. But we believe current market pricing for a series of rate hikes appears somewhat aggressive:

The ECB is taking a meeting-by-meeting approach. President Christine Lagarde stressed that uncertainty remains exceptionally high and that the Governing Council needs more evidence on how the energy shock will feed through to broader inflation before taking further action. The ECB offered no explicit forward guidance and repeated its meeting-by-meeting approach.

Lagarde noted that underlying price growth has stayed “contained.” Headline inflation has delivered encouraging news, with second-quarter readings coming in slightly weaker than the ECB’s staff projections. Core inflation is less benign, with services inflation running above 3%, but it remains broadly in line with the ECB’s staff projections made in June. Inflation expectations also remain anchored. We believe a September move is firmly

Summer, sunshine, and perspective Weekly viewpoints Burkhard Varnholt, Senior Financial Market Adviser, UBS Switzerland AG

Today: Two old paradoxes offer encouragement for the future. They show why AI is opening new paths—and creating additional jobs. And the rhythm and blues earworm “Ain’t No Stoppin’ Us Now” lifts the mood and describes why shoppers are the driving force and expression of our “Roaring Twenties” scenario. For anyone looking for variety this weekend, we recommend a scenic, mostly crowd-free two-day hike in Switzerland. Lace up your shoes and switch off.

1. Paradox: Why AI creates additional jobs Agatha Christie once noted that she had never expected to become rich enough to own a car—or poor enough to no longer have servants: “I couldn’t imagine being too poor to afford servants, nor so rich as to be able to afford a car.”

That this sentence strikes us today as a curiosity is due to two paradoxes often cited in the tech world: the Jevons paradox and the Baumol paradox. Both explain why technological disruptions have often been misunderstood throughout history. Since the start of industrialization, people have feared that technological progress would put jobs at risk. Ultimately, the “human versus machine” debate is as old as the cultural history of the modern era.

Last week, I discussed it with several European entrepreneurs. The conclusion was clear: AI, too, is a job engine that will change many jobs but, on balance, create more work than it eliminates. The thesis may be provocative, but it is supported by facts and principles1. “Technology has never permanently destroyed jobs, but has always created new ones,” explained Nobel laureate in economics Paul Romer2, who has spent his career studying the interaction between ideas, growth, and labor markets. Let us look at the Jevons and Baumol paradoxes.

Jevons paradox: How AI creates far more jobs than it destroys In 1865, William Stanley Jevons (1835-1882) argued that technological advances that make resource use more efficient can, paradoxically, increase total consumption of that resource rather than reduce it. His observation— now known as the Jevons paradox—is often cited by tech executives such as Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella to justify the massive expansion of data centers: “The more efficiency, the more use—we will not get enough of it.”
1 BCG (3 April 2026): AI Will Reshape More Jobs Than It Replaces 2 Romer, Paul M. (1990): “Endogenous Technological Change.” Journal of Political Economy,
This report has been prepared by UBS Switzerland AG. Please see important disclaimers and disclosures at the end of the document.

In 1965—exactly 100 years later—William Jack Baumol described a second paradox, the so-called cost disease, which explains why the current AI boom does not replace some skilled manual activities but, on the contrary, makes them more expensive. Both paradoxes illustrate AI’s influence on the modern working world—and put the contradictory views of it into perspective.

Jevons’ gloomy 1865 book, The Coal Question, predicted the end of British prosperity because of coal shortages. Efficiency, he argued, was not a way out: “It is a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth.” If the efficiency of the steam engine doubles, less coal is not burned—more machines are built, and more coal is ultimately consumed. Jevons was wrong with his gloomy economic forecast—poverty caused by coal shortages—but not with the logic of rising consumption.

A present-day example: LEDs require about 15% of the energy used by an incandescent bulb. So do we save 85% of energy? At the start of their invention, yes. But then we installed more lights, left them on longer, and built, for example, the Las Vegas Sphere, whose gigantic LED wall— the largest in the world—alone consumes as much electricity as 50,000 households.

Professor Erik Brynjolfsson of Stanford University puts it this way: “Pilots became dramatically more productive with the jet. Did that mean we needed fewer pilots? No. We simply decided to fly much more.”…
marketdesk-jftebbbjnyi-71f35b: Oil has rallied hard, but the story is more nuanced than simply "war equals higher prices." Technicals suggest the move is becoming stretched, while JPMorgan argues the market has remained balanced through weaker demand rather than collapsing supply. The key question now is whether that adjustment can continue if disruptions persist.

The surge in oil has pushed RSI into deeply overbought territory. While the Middle East situation remains highly fluid, the market looks due for at least a short-term pause. Whether that pause turns into another leg higher depends largely on the fundamental backdrop outlined below.

Oil volatility has picked up in recent weeks, but remains well below the levels seen during the March panic despite the sharp rally in spot prices. The key difference is that this move has been a steady grind higher rather than a series of panic-driven spikes, something that tends to keep implied volatility more contained.

The latest escalation in the Middle East has pushed Brent nearly 40% higher in July, on track for its strongest monthly gain since March, while US gasoline prices have climbed back above $4 per gallon. Yet at around $100/bbl, Brent is only about $13 above JPMorgan's estimated fair value, suggesting the market is pricing in only a modest geopolitical risk premium. That is notable given tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains at just 50% of pre-war levels, far below JPMorgan's assumption of a recovery toward roughly 73%, with even rerouted pipeline flows facing growing disruption risks.

Despite severe disruptions to shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb and Strait of Hormuz, oil prices remain relatively subdued. Partly, markets appear to be pricing in a negotiated resolution rather than a prolonged conflict. More importantly, the market has rebalanced through weaker demand rather than inventory draws. Since the conflict began, roughly 11.1 mbd of supply has been lost, but demand has fallen by about 5.1 mbd, offsetting nearly half of that loss, while inventory releases contributed only 3.6 mbd. Because the adjustment has come primarily from weaker consumption rather than depleted inventories, oil prices have remained lower than many expected.

The magnitude of the estimated demand loss has raised questions, especially with the global economy still growing above trend. While hidden inventory draws, particularly in China and other countries with limited reporting, could explain part of the gap, JPMorgan believes most of the adjustment reflects genuine demand losses caused by physical supply shortages rather than higher prices. The burden fell overwhelmingly on non-OECD countries and China, where limited access to alternative supplies forced fuel rationing and petrochemical shutdowns. OECD demand proved far more resilient, with US oil consumption even rising during the FIFA World Cup. China ultimately absorbed most of the shock, cutting oil imports by roughly 5 million barrels, while the US and Japan supplemented the adjustment through large strategic inventory releases.

JPMorgan argues the current disruptions are not yet enough to create a severe global supply shortage. Even if flows through Hormuz and the Red Sea decline by another 4 mbd, the market could remain balanced provided demand, especially in China, stays depressed. China is expected to sustain crude imports roughly 4 mbd below normal for another three months, continuing to cushion the market. Over time, however, inventories would need to shoulder a much larger burden. A three-month extension of the conflict would require nearly 500 million additional barrels of inventory releases on top of the roughly 500 million barrels already drawn down. JPMorgan warns the US has limited capacity to keep supplying that buffer, meaning Europe, Japan and South Korea would increasingly need to release inventories, or global demand would have to weaken further.

Tracking Rising Equity Allocations for Asset Owners

As we wrote in our recent Global Strategy Paper: Balancing Innovation and Inflation in Portfolios, the value of global financial assets has had a material boost from strong equity returns in the last 3-4 years. In fact, the performance of equities vs. bonds since the GFC has been close to the very high ex post equity risk premia last seen during the Golden 1920s and 1950s – and ex post equity risk premia have been above Tech Bubble levels as equity returns have been stronger for longer. Most recently, AI capex-related stocks globally have led equities higher.

As a result, global financial assets as tracked by our World Portfolio benchmark (see also the proxy GSMBWP01, developed by GS Global Banking & Markets) have drifted materially towards equities, in particular the Tech sector. Similar market value-weighted benchmarks tend to influence investor asset allocations as size indicates importance and liquidity of assets. Thus, prolonged trends in asset performance are not just driving shifts in global financial assets but tend to be a key driver of investor asset allocations. In this Global Markets Daily we track changing asset allocations for asset owners globally and investigate the drivers.

Our baseline predicated on our more benign inflation outlook than the SARB’s — assuming a moderation in oil prices — is for rates on hold and a resumption of easing in Q1 2027, even if we see some near-term risk of a rate hike in September (depending on oil prices and the Rand).

1. The SARB kept its policy rate on hold at +7.00%, in line with our forecast, but in a downside surprise to market pricing and consensus expectations for a 25bp hike (17 out of 20 analysts surveyed by Bloomberg forecast a hike). The decision resulted from a 4-2 split vote within the MPC (with two hawkish dissents in favour of a hike) and follows from a 25bp rate hike in May (also resulting from a 4-2 split vote, but with two dovish dissents). 2. With respect to inflation, the statement notes a slight improvement to the outlook since the May MPC and the SARB has reduced its near-term inflation forecasts, largely on lower food and fuel inflation. marketdesk-lx9tflwvgf8-fe2849: The recent rise in oil has spilled over into rates, with bond volatility beginning to respond. While the MOVE Index remains well below panic levels, the recent acceleration is worth monitoring given its historical relationship with equities.

Rates have continued to climb, flirting with a major breakout. The initial move higher was accompanied by unusually complacent bond volatility, but that has started to change. The MOVE Index has caught a strong bid recently, marking its largest cumulative advance since mid-May.

The oil squeeze is spilling into rates, and rates are beginning to spill into bond volatility. But unlike the initial oil panic, the MOVE Index is reacting in a far more orderly fashion, a sign the bond market isn't pricing a full-blown shock just yet.
Both the MOVE Index and the VIX have moved higher lately, but the rise in bond volatility has been considerably more pronounced. It's another sign that stress is building first in rates.

Equities rarely enjoy sharp spikes in bond volatility. Historically, equities have struggled when bond volatility accelerates. For now, stocks remain relatively resilient, but that divergence may not persist if the MOVE Index continues to climb.

Healey has brought the defence-funding dispute into the Treasury, despite Burnham’s focus on domestic priorities. The £15bn DIP uplift offers a modest near-term boost; the larger return depends on private investment and R&D. Manchesterism and BoE easing could support that response, while Gilts judge the capacity created against the borrowing required.

Burnham’s unspoken theory of economic revival may now be taking shape around defence. The Greater Manchester model uses public procurement to give firms the confidence to invest, while planning, skills, transport, and housing help workers and businesses build around that demand. Burnham has placed little public emphasis on defence investment, yet his appointment of John Healey as finance minister (Chancellor of the Exchequer) suggests that incremental military spending could become the central government vehicle for a national rollout. The current Defence Investment Plan (DIP) adds only £15bn over four years and is financed largely through reallocations, leaving a modest near-term growth impulse. But, the stronger case rests on predictable orders “crowding in” private investment and R&D - with further success relying on cheaper energy to industrial consumers and Bank of England easing, as inflation permits. The UK government bond market will judge the productive capacity created against the additional borrowing, imports and cost pressure.

John Healey resigned as Defence Secretary after concluding that the DIP was inadequately funded and poorly configured for the wars Britain was preparing to fight. Five weeks later, he controls the Treasury. Andy Burnham has appointed him Chancellor and described the decision to NATO Secretary- General Mark Rutte as a “signal of intent”, despite entering Downing Street with an agenda centred on household support, stronger public control and reindustrialisation through public procurement. Defence featured as an international obligation that Burnham’s domestic reforms would allow Britain to honour, rather than a defining priority of the new government.

Healey’s position is harder to reconcile with continuity. He argued that the DIP lacked the scale, speed and mix of capabilities required, but can now no longer blame the Treasury for blocking additional resources. As Defence Secretary, he also supported UK participation in the proposed Defence, Security and Resilience Bank(DSRB), with his allies claiming that the Treasury tried to close down the initiative. His successor, Wes Streeting, has already made reconsidering membership an “early priority”, citing
the prospect of cheaper and more accessible finance for defence SMEs. Healey now controls the institution that resisted his proposal.

my instincts remain the same: simplify your portfolio and concentrate risk in the highest conviction parts of it.

marketdesk-pbrqy0j6xai-3993d6: Surprise July Rate Hike Would Upend Risk Sentiment

BY TYLER DURDEN THURSDAY, JUL 23, 2026 - 07:10 PM Authored by Michael Ball, Bloomberg macro strategist, Markets may be underpricing a July Fed hike, given still-high inflation, a steady economic backdrop, a growing committee quorum and a strong credibility incentive to move sooner and ultimately have to tighten policy less later. A surprise hike would weigh on risk sentiment, flatten the Treasury curve, move the dollar higher and weigh on duration sensitive assets. June’s inflation readings were soft enough to knock the odds of a Fed hike in July close to 10% at one point. However, that didn’t settle the debate. A renewed Iran conflict has revived energy shock risks, and reminded markets that core PCE remains materially above 2%. Inflation worries have been further reinforced by the AI-capex pulse and accommodative financial conditions. As a result, the pricing of a Fed rate hike has been steadily rising into the July FOMC meeting, and now is over 35%...

Economic growth offers little reason to wait, as well. Real final domestic demand is running near 3% in the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow tracker, business investment is accelerating and the labor market looks stable, according to the Fed’s own staff assessment and recent speeches. That gives the Fed cover to prioritize inflation. Warsh’s own recent Congressional testimony raises the cost of delay. He told Congress the economy is solid, warned against financial conditions feeding boom-bust cycles and argued that monetary policy should serve the real economy rather than Wall Street. He also blamed the prior 75 bps of cuts for helping inflation move further above target without sustaining employment. Delaying a hike after such forceful testimony would weaken the chairman’s credibility. A July hike would also align better with the political cycle, as not to shock the market closer to the midterms in November. The FOMC votes look available. marketdesk-px1bqzeoemw-0f599b: Gold To Show Resilience On Reserves, Debt Burdens

BY TYLER DURDEN THURSDAY, JUL 23, 2026 - 05:50 PM Authored by Garfield Reynolds via Bloomberg, Gold’s worst days are probably over as central banks keep buying the precious metal. The prospect of swelling sovereign bond issuance is also reviving its appeal as a hedge against the risk that governments will inflate away their debt burdens. Bullion has risen in July, trading above $4,100 an ounce, to head for its first month of gains since the Middle East war began. That’s even as renewed hostilities between the US and Iran have caused crude oil prices to surge again following a two-month slump. Gold’s advance signals investors may be returning to the metal as a diversification play as uncertainty over the war’s future mounts again, President Trump moves to revive his tariff plans and questions linger about the sustainability of the AI-led boom. The March-June slide in gold prices led more central banks than ever to say that they expect to increase holdings, which are about 10 times as large as the gold held in ETFs. China’s central bank added to its stockpile in June for a 20th straight month, with its biggest purchase since 2023. Poland is on pace to match its 2025 effort, when it reported buying more gold than any other central bank.

The long-term bull case for gold owes much to expectations for sustained demand from determined buy-and-hold types. That centers on deep-pocketed central banks and those retail investors who perceive it as an alternative to most financial assets. Bullion’s relatively stable supply, along with minimal counterparty risk, makes it attractive for investors with longer time horizons. Such buyers lean on the yellow metal’s hefty outperformance relative to equities this millennium, even taking into account a “lost decade.” Those are the sort of buyers who came to the fore in recent years when gold posted stunning gains despite higher real yields and a stronger US dollar, dynamics that had previously been regarded as certain to bring precious metals lower. The overall pace of gold buying by central banks sped up in the first quarter of 2026, with net official-sector purchases totaling 244 tons versus 208 tons in the previous quarter, according to estimates from the World Gold Council. That’s even as Turkey, Russia and Azerbaijan sold the precious metal for their own specific reasons. Meanwhile, speculators who began 2026 by piling into gold as prices more than doubled in the previous three years, abandoned the trade as the metal sank after the war fueled rate-hike bets, dimming the appeal of non-yielding bullion. ETF holdings also started to decline, highlighting the likelihood that financial investors more generally had turned away from gold as a momentum play.

marketdesk-romgvlkmfpn-86c58d: Oil continues to dominate the macro narrative, but beneath the surface several other themes are gaining importance. AI financing is becoming a growing concern for credit markets, rate expectations are shifting higher, technicals across semiconductors continue to weaken, while an oversold setup and favorable seasonality suggest a short-term bounce in Nasdaq cannot be ruled out.
The surge in oil has led the RSI to hit very overbought levels. The ME situation remains very fluid, but oil is desperate for a pause, at least in the short term.

The latest escalation in the Middle East has pushed Brent nearly 40% higher in July, on track for its strongest monthly gain since March, while US gasoline prices have climbed back above $4 per gallon. Yet at around $100/bbl, Brent is only about $13 above JPMorgan's estimated fair value, suggesting the market is pricing in only a modest geopolitical risk premium. That is notable given tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains at just 50% of pre-war levels, far below JPMorgan's assumption of a recovery toward roughly 73%, with even rerouted pipeline flows facing growing disruption risks.

JPMorgan estimates Brent would average around $94 if the conflict is contained within a month. However, each additional month of disruptions adds roughly $7–8/bbl as global inventories become increasingly depleted, pushing Brent toward $114 if the conflict lasts three months. A rebound in Chinese crude imports would add further upside, with every 1 mbd increase lifting fair value by roughly $3/bbl. The same dynamic applies to gasoline. Under a prolonged disruption, US gasoline prices could rise from around $4.20 after one month to above $4.50 after two months, a level that has historically increased pressure for policymakers to pursue negotiations. More on oil here.

While hyperscalers have strong balance sheets and ample financial flexibility, the market is becoming less forgiving of ever-rising AI spending. The pressure is already visible in credit markets. Meta's $27.3 billion Hyperion financing was issued at par, traded above 109, and has since fallen to around 97. The broader concern is deteriorating free cash flow conversion as capex accelerates. Increasingly, investing in hyperscalers is a bet that AI revenues ramp before spending peaks. If not, today's capacity build could become tomorrow's compute oversupply, just as much larger depreciation charges begin flowing through income statements, writes Privorotsky. Latest note here.

Google encapsulated the market's growing concern around AI spending. Despite reporting excellent operating results, including 82% Cloud growth, Alphabet fell 6.9% after raising 2026 capex guidance to $195–205 billion and posting negative quarterly free cash flow of $5.9 billion. Investors are becoming less willing to treat AI spending as costless, particularly as questions around long-term returns remain unanswered. More importantly, higher spending by Google raises the bar for the rest of the hyperscalers, increasing pressure across the sector, writes Privorotsky. Together, these developments suggest AI is increasingly becoming a credit story rather than just an equity story. As capex accelerates and debt issuance climbs, investors are beginning to focus less on AI revenue potential and more on how the buildout is being financed.

AI is no longer just driving equity markets, it's reshaping credit. Goldman Sachs notes that investment- grade issuance is increasingly outpacing US Treasury supply, fueled by record debt issuance from AI hyperscalers. The question is no longer whether they can borrow, but whether this torrent of new bonds starts crowding out the rest of the market.

A changing world (dis)order: risks and opportunities Weekly - Regional View Swiss Michael Bolliger, Chief Investment Officer Switzerland, UBS Switzerland AG
• The current global order is multipolar, fragmented, and marked by numerous risks.
• However, headlines should not prompt investors to react in the short term; what matters is a systematic assessment of the causes, interconnections, and long-term effects.
• This should enable risks to be mitigated effectively without overlooking the potential offered by structural opportunities.

The news is teeming with crisis headlines every day: the war in the Middle East, tensions between the US and China, threats of punitive tariffs, debt or government crises, rising competitive pressure from China, and even the football World Cup has been accused of being influenced by political forces. The topics change, but the sense of uncertainty remains. The world appears to be in transition, and because of the complexity and interconnectedness of these developments, it is becoming increasingly difficult to assess them. This often also affects investment decisions.

An effective strategy for investors is not to attach too much importance to such headlines, in our view. However, those who still wish to engage with these topics would be well advised to do so systematically. The World Economic Forum’s annual “Global Risks Report” is one of many sources of this type of analysis, assessing the relevance of developments, looking for causes, and highlighting interdependencies. This could enable investors not only to better assess risks, but also to recognize the opportunities that arise from them.

Fundamentally, the point is that the world order is indeed changing, and the causes are varied. The WEF distinguishes between geopolitical, economic, societal, technological, and environmental drivers.

This diversity is unlikely to change much in the coming years. Issues such as the targeted use of tariffs, sanctions, export controls or subsidies, geopolitical confrontation, armed conflicts, deliberate misinformation, and increasing social polarization will likely continue to be front of mind for investors in the years ahead. Extreme weather events such as floods, heatwaves, or storms are also likely to be on that list, with potentially negative consequences for people, infrastructure, and the economy. Technology and innovation also play a decisive role. Developments in artificial intelligence and various other key technologies, such as quantum computing and the race for dominance in

The roots of this change are not only diverse; they are also interconnected. A war or sanctions are often only the proverbial tip of the iceberg. Behind it lie deeper, often complex and long-term developments that are favored and reinforced by shifts in power and multilateralism. On the one hand, the world is moving away from a clear, US-dominated order toward a multipolar, fragmented structure. This allows regional actors to set new rules, while the once-established standards for cooperation and trade may also change. This comes alongside the declining effectiveness of international institutions, which can make it harder to find common solutions to global issues such as climate, debt, or security. At the same time, growing inequality is intensifying social tensions, weakening trust in politics and institutions, and increasing vulnerability to populism and polarization. Added to this is the potential influence of artificial intelligence, cyber risks, and new technologies on labor markets, information flows, and security structures.

But she also stressed that the flaring up of the conflict had led to serious developments in commodities markets. We believe distinguishing between aggregate shocks to the overall value of AI and distributional shocks to how that value is shared is critical for understanding market vulnerabilities and hedging strategies. Aggregate shocks, such as slower adoption rates or macro tightening, reduce the total expected value of AI gains, broadly impacting US equities, pushing yields lower, and driving index volatility higher. Conversely, distributional shocks, like shifts in capital spending beneficiaries or increased competition, reallocate value among hyperscalers and suppliers with limited cross-asset or index-level impacts. Consequently, investors with broad equity exposure can effectively use macro assets to hedge aggregate risks, while those with concentrated AI positions face greater challenges protecting against distributional shifts. Shifts in platinum ETF holdings by regions since start of 2025 Last year, platinum recorded modest ETF inflows of around 51,000 ounces. Values are in thousand ounces So far this year, however, platinum ETF holdings have declined by roughly 515,000 ounces to 2.8 million ounces. In our view, the more interesting aspect of ETF holdings is the regional split. Europe-based platinum ETFs declined between June and July last year and have remained broadly stable since. Africa-based platinum ETFs began to see larger outflows in January this year. These ETFs are denominated in local currencies, and with platinum reaching a record high in South African rand terms, profit-taking is likely the main driver of the decline.

By contrast, North America-based platinum ETFs continued to record inflows until February this year. Since March, however, these ETFs have Source: Bloomberg, UBS experienced sizable outflows. We believe two factors drove last year’s inflows. First, concerns that the US might impose tariffs on platinum imports, which ultimately did not materialize. And second, investor buying following the European Commission’s decision to soften the ban on sales of internal combustion engine vehicles in the European Union from 2035. This, however, will not affect demand in the near term. Higher oil prices, market pricing of US rate hikes this year, and weaker precious metals prices likely prompted North American investors to reduce their platinum ETF holdings this year.

Given weak jewelry and investment demand, there is a risk that the platinum market could move into a surplus this year. However, given our expectation that gold prices will rise over the coming months, we retain a moderately constructive outlook for platinum.

In addition, Chinese AI firms spend a fraction of what US hyperscalers deploy (see Figure 2). By most headline public benchmarks, many Chinese models also trail the leading US models—even if the gap has narrowed materially.1 In short, the market has tended to view China as lagging where investors have so far placed the highest premium in the AI trade: the semiconductor supply chain, large-scale frontier data centers, and model leadership. We argue here that China’s position in the AI race should be rethought. We Strategy & Insights think this is driven in large part by US-led export restrictions designed to slow China’s progress in AI.
